channel.title: Chaosmos blog
channel.description: How the Chaosmos puzzle games get made: devlogs, design notes, the maths behind the levels, and news.

item.title: Two weeks in: where our games stand before launch
item.description: A short update before launch: where our games are, what is new in them, one bug I liked, and what comes next at Chaosmos.

item.title: How I build games with Claude
item.description: Chaosmos is one person working with an AI model. What I do, what Claude does, how a change gets to my phone, how it is checked, and what goes wrong.

item.title: Calm by design: why our games never rush you
item.description: No timers, no lives, no energy and no ad in the middle of a puzzle. How Plumb, Carillon and Apsis leave you room to think, and where the ads do go.

item.title: Proven solvable: how our games build their own levels
item.description: Plumb, Carillon and Apsis all follow one rule: a program makes every level and another proves it. Here is how each game does it, and why it matters.

item.title: Meet Chaosmos: puzzle games, made one at a time
item.description: Chaosmos is a small studio making calm, clever puzzle games. Here is what I make, how I make it, and what is coming next.

item.title: Every tile earns its place: inside Plumb's level generator
item.description: How Plumb's levels are made: random boards, a solver that sets the goal, a test that each chapter's rule matters, and a pass that strips tiles the best route never needs.

item.title: Fields grown from roots: how Carillon builds a level
item.description: How Carillon grows each field from roots, dresses it with its chapter's rule, proves the goal with a solver, measures difficulty in bits and turns away repeats.

item.title: Built backwards: how every Apsis sky is made clearable
item.description: How Apsis builds each level backwards so it can always be cleared, aims arrows to block, measures difficulty in reads, orders the levels and refuses repeats.

item.title: Why the Apsis hint is never wrong
item.description: What the Apsis hint lights, why a free arrow is always a safe move, how it picks among free arrows, and what it does at a jam or when you are out of hearts.

item.title: Where Plumb's goal comes from, and how to reach it
item.description: Plumb's goal is the fewest tilts a solver could find, not a guess. How it is worked out, how stars are counted against it, and a way to reach it more often.

item.title: Chain reactions as graphs: the maths behind a Carillon tap
item.description: A Carillon field is a directed graph, a chain is a shortest-path search, and the goal is a count of source components, right up until the rules start to bend it.

item.title: Straight lines across circles: the geometry inside Apsis
item.description: How Apsis works out exactly what a flying arrow hits, why an arrow along its ring catches the one ahead, how close arrows pass the sun, and which arrow you meant.

item.title: The best next tap: inside Carillon's hint
item.description: What Carillon's hint lights up, how the solver picks one dot from the field as it stands, what a hint costs, and how to use it to learn a field rather than skip it.

item.title: Why four directions go so deep: the maths of tilting
item.description: Plumb has only four moves, yet its longest levels take over twenty tilts. How moving every marble at once grows a vast tree of sequences that folds into few positions.

item.title: Habits that save hearts in Apsis
item.description: Ways of reading an Apsis sky that keep your hearts: trace every line first, trust the band over the line, doubt arrows pointing out, and read the marks.

item.title: Pits, undo and restart: Plumb lets you be wrong
item.description: How Plumb's square pits work, what Undo and Restart give back, and how to use them to explore a board, since a mistake costs one tap and nothing else.

item.title: What the spare tap is for: stars in Carillon
item.description: How Carillon scores a level against its goal, why every level gives you one spare tap, what the pips and the star meter are saying, and how to find the three-star read.

item.title: Hearts, misses and stars: how Apsis keeps score
item.description: Apsis never counts your taps. It counts misses: how three hearts become stars, what a miss costs, the hearts a level means you to spend, and retrying.

item.title: Reach, sources and decoys: reading a Carillon field
item.description: How to read a Carillon field before you tap: trace the reach circles, find the dots nothing reaches, look past the showy decoys and, once rules arrive, plan the order.

item.title: Ghost marbles: what Plumb's hint shows, and why
item.description: Plumb's hint draws your best next tilt on the board with trails, ghost marbles and rings. What each mark means, how the solver picks it, and how to learn from it.

item.title: What is an apsis? The astronomy behind the name
item.description: An apsis is the point of an orbit nearest to or farthest from the body it goes around. Periapsis, apoapsis, perihelion and apogee, and why a puzzle game took the name.

item.title: Read the roll before you tilt: habits for new Plumb players
item.description: Ways of looking at a Plumb board that make levels click: find the stops, judge a tilt by every marble, distrust the easy drop, and ask what each tile is for.

item.title: Why every pop is a note: the pentatonic idea behind Carillon
item.description: In Carillon a dot's colour is its note and its size is the octave, on a pentatonic scale, so any chain sounds like music. How the notes are chosen, made and played.

item.title: Every arrow wants out: the rules of Apsis
item.description: Learn Apsis on its first five skies: tap an arrow and it flies straight out if its way is clear, or bounces back and costs one of your three hearts.

item.title: One tap, a whole chain: how a Carillon field works
item.description: Learn Carillon by following one chain across the first field: a ring pops every dot it reaches, every pop rings a note, and reading the field is the whole game.

item.title: Learn Plumb in one board: tilt, roll, drop
item.description: Plumb's rules, taught by its first real boards: swipe to tilt, every marble rolls until something stops it, and each one drops into the hole of its own colour.
